strengths: The paper targets an important and relatively underexplored setting: panoramic semantic scene completion for legged/humanoid robots under gait-induced motion. This is a meaningful departure from the dominant forward-facing autonomous-driving SSC setup.

The proposed benchmarks are potentially valuable. QuadOcc provides real first-person 360-degree quadruped data with day/dusk/night coverage, and H3O adds controlled synthetic human-ego splits including within-city and cross-city evaluation.

The system is coherent: dual raw/equirectangular processing, Cartesian plus cylindrical voxelization, pre-lifting displacement compensation, and hierarchical 3D fusion are well motivated for panoramic geometry and full-surround perception.

Experiments are reasonably broad within the authors' proposed setting, including LiDAR and vision baselines, per-class IoUs, lighting-condition analysis, component ablations, qualitative examples, and runtime/memory reporting.

Results show consistent gains over adapted vision baselines, especially on H3O cross-city (+8.08 mIoU over MonoScene), and the ablation table indicates additive improvements from the proposed modules.
weaknesses: The main algorithmic novelty is moderate. Most components resemble known ideas adapted to this domain: multi-projection processing, cylindrical/polar grids, attention/MoE 3D fusion, and zero-initialized displacement heads. The contribution is more an integration for a new setting than a clearly new technical principle.

The strongest empirical claims rely almost entirely on newly introduced datasets. There is no evaluation on established panoramic/occupancy benchmarks or external real-world datasets, making it hard to separate method quality from dataset-specific design choices.

QuadOcc is small and narrow for a real benchmark: 10 scenes on a campus, 6 semantic classes, and a low 64x64x8 grid. The reported mIoU gains on QuadOcc are modest (+1.37 over MonoScene), and OneOcc is worse than MonoScene at night, which weakens the robustness claim.

The LiDAR comparison is not fully convincing. The paper claims camera-only OneOcc surpasses popular LiDAR methods, but the LiDAR baselines may be disadvantaged by the low-resolution voxel setup, limited class set, and adaptation details; SGN with LiDAR has better geometry IoU and is close in mIoU.

The Gait Displacement Compensation mechanism is under-validated. It predicts a global 2D offset from a single image feature map without explicit temporal, IMU, or gait phase input; the QuadOcc ablation gain is only +0.39 mIoU, and there is no analysis by motion severity or learned displacement behavior.

Dataset construction and annotation reliability need more evidence. QuadOcc uses multi-frame LiDAR aggregation, Grounded-SAM initialization, and manual fixes, but the manuscript does not sufficiently quantify annotation quality, dynamic-object handling, calibration errors, or inter-annotator/verification procedures.

Efficiency claims are overstated. A 101.76M-parameter model is not obviously lightweight for onboard legged robotics, and the Jetson Thor FPS estimate is a speculative linear TFLOPS extrapolation involving sparsity assumptions rather than a real deployment measurement.

Reproducibility is only partially supported. The paper states code and datasets will be released, but key implementation details for adapting baselines, training schedules, H3O gait simulation, LiDAR aggregation, and calibration/visibility masks are not detailed enough to independently reproduce the claims from the manuscript alone.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored setting: panoramic semantic scene completion for legged/humanoid platforms, where full 360-degree perception and body motion differ from standard autonomous-driving SSC assumptions.

The proposed benchmarks, QuadOcc and Human360Occ, are potentially useful. A real quadruped panoramic dataset with day/dusk/night coverage and a CARLA human-ego panoramic benchmark could help the community study non-car occupancy perception if released with sufficient documentation.

The method is engineering-practical and modular. Dual raw/equirectangular processing, Cartesian/cylindrical voxelization, feature-level displacement correction, and a lightweight 3D decoder are plausible design choices for panoramic SSC.
The experiments include several relevant SSC baselines and report both real and simulated settings, within-city and cross-city splits, lighting breakdowns, per-class IoUs, and component ablations.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. Most core ingredients appear to be combinations of known ideas: dual projections for omnidirectional images, cylindrical/polar grids, attention-style 3D fusion, and MoE gating. The paper does not convincingly establish which part is a substantive new contribution beyond adapting existing components to panoramas.

The central claim of gait robustness is weakly supported. GDC is described as a global 2D displacement regressed from single-frame features, without direct gait phase, temporal modeling, IMU/odometry input, or quantitative evaluation under controlled motion amplitudes. The paper claims correction of gait-induced jitter, but does not show that the learned offsets correspond to real motion or outperform stronger motion/pose compensation baselines.

The empirical margins on the real dataset are modest. On QuadOcc, OneOcc improves over MonoScene by only +1.37 mIoU and is worse on some major classes such as road and vegetation. It also trails MonoScene at night. These mixed results do not fully support the broad claims of robust legged-robot perception.

The comparison to LiDAR methods is overstated. The paper claims a camera-only model rivals or surpasses LiDAR stacks, but the evaluation uses a small, low-resolution 64x64x8 grid and only selected classic LiDAR baselines. Stronger or more recent LiDAR/multimodal baselines are missing, and the fairness of adapting LiDAR methods to this dataset is not sufficiently documented.

Dataset and annotation details are insufficient for judging reliability. QuadOcc has only 10 scenes, uses semi-automatic labels from multi-frame LiDAR aggregation plus Grounded-SAM and manual fixes, but the manuscript gives little information about annotation error, temporal alignment, calibration quality, train/val scene separation, class imbalance handling, or inter-annotator/quality control. These issues matter because the reported gains are small.

Baseline tuning and reproducibility are under-specified. The paper says training follows official configs with minimal changes, but does not give enough detail on input resolutions, depth predictors, schedule parity, augmentation, backbone choices, hyperparameters, random seeds, or variance. No confidence intervals or multi-seed results are reported.

The ablation is too incremental to justify the architecture. Component gains on QuadOcc are small: +0.39, +0.31, +0.41, and +0.26 mIoU. There is no ablation isolating raw vs equirectangular without GDC, polar grid cost/benefit, number of experts, or displacement behavior, and no comparable ablation on H3O.

Efficiency claims are not convincing. A 101.76M parameter model running at about 14 FPS FP32 or 19 FPS mixed precision on an RTX 4090 is not clearly lightweight for onboard legged robotics. The Jetson Thor estimate is a linear extrapolation from peak tensor throughput with sparsity assumptions, not a measured deployment result.

The paper contains presentation and professionalism issues that reduce confidence: the code URL is blank, Figure 2 contains non-English text and typos, several terms are inconsistently named, and some claims such as 'strong distribution robustness' exceed the evidence presented.

Overall, the work has a useful problem setting and possible dataset value, but the supported scientific contribution is not yet strong enough for acceptance. The main concerns are limited originality, overclaimed robustness, weak support for the gait-compensation mechanism, insufficient dataset/annotation validation, and under-specified experimental fairness.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: full-surround semantic scene completion for legged/humanoid robots using a single panoramic camera, where gait motion and 360-degree continuity make standard autonomous-driving SSC assumptions less suitable.

The benchmark contribution is valuable. QuadOcc provides real quadruped panoramic occupancy data, while Human360Occ adds controlled synthetic human-ego data with within-city and cross-city splits; together they create a useful testbed for this niche but practically relevant setting.

The proposed architecture is well motivated by the sensing geometry: dual raw/equirectangular projections, Cartesian plus cylindrical voxelization, and multi-scale 3D fusion are sensible design choices for panoramic occupancy.

The experimental evidence is reasonably broad for a new benchmark paper: the authors retrain several LiDAR and camera SSC baselines, report per-class IoU and geometry metrics, include lighting-condition analysis, qualitative comparisons, and component ablations.

Results are consistently positive. OneOcc improves mIoU over the strongest camera baseline on QuadOcc by 1.37, on H3O within-city by 3.83, and on H3O cross-city by 8.08, suggesting the design is especially useful under distribution shift.
weaknesses: The real-world validation remains limited: QuadOcc has only 10 scenes from a campus domain, 6 classes, and a coarse 64x64x8 grid. This supports the proposed setting, but it is not yet strong evidence of broad deployment robustness for diverse legged-robot environments.

The gait-robustness claim is only partially supported. GDC gives a small ablation gain on QuadOcc (+0.39 mIoU), and the paper does not provide direct analysis versus measured gait phase, jitter magnitude, temporal instability, calibration drift, or comparisons to IMU/odometry-based compensation.

Some comparisons need more caution. The claim that camera-only OneOcc surpasses LiDAR baselines may be specific to this low-resolution benchmark and the adapted baseline implementations; the paper does not establish that the LiDAR models are optimally tuned for panoramic robot data.

The method is a composition of plausible existing ideas rather than a sharply new technical principle: dual projections, cylindrical grids, attention/MoE fusion, and coordinate warping are individually familiar. The novelty is mainly in their integration for this setting plus the datasets.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the manuscript: the code URL is blank, dataset annotation quality/control procedures are not deeply specified, and training hyperparameters/splits are summarized only briefly. This is especially important because both benchmarks are new.

The efficiency discussion is somewhat overstated. A 101.76M-parameter model is not obviously lightweight for onboard legged robotics, and the Jetson Thor estimate is a simple FLOP scaling extrapolation rather than an actual embedded benchmark.

Presentation has several polish issues, including missing/garbled table legend symbols, a non-English phrase in Figure 2, spacing/formatting artifacts, and occasional overclaiming such as “severe body jitter” without commensurate empirical stress tests. These do not invalidate the work but reduce confidence and clarity.

strengths: The paper targets an underexplored and practically important setting: 360-degree semantic occupancy for legged/humanoid robots from a single panoramic camera, with gait-induced motion and full-surround perception explicitly considered.

The benchmark contribution is substantial. QuadOcc provides real quadruped PAL-camera data with synchronized LiDAR-derived occupancy, and H3O provides a larger controlled CARLA benchmark with within-city and cross-city splits, weather/lighting variation, depth, pose, and two voxel resolutions.

The method is well motivated for panoramic geometry: dual raw/equirectangular processing, Cartesian plus cylindrical voxelization, feature-level gait displacement compensation, and a lightweight 3D decoder each address plausible failure modes of standard monocular SSC pipelines.

The experimental section is broad. The paper retrains several vision and LiDAR SSC baselines, reports per-class IoU, lighting robustness, within/cross-city generalization, ablations, efficiency, Jetson runtime, calibration-noise robustness, temporal aggregation, FoV, grid resolution, and projection-path studies.

The strongest results are meaningful on H3O, especially the cross-city setting where OneOcc improves over MonoScene by 8.08 mIoU, suggesting that the geometry-aware panoramic design helps distribution robustness.
The supplementary implementation and dataset-construction details are unusually extensive, which improves reproducibility if the promised code and data are released.
weaknesses: The real-data evaluation is still narrow: QuadOcc has only 10 campus-like scenes, 6 semantic classes, a low 64x64x8 grid, and heavy day dominance. This limits the strength of claims about general legged/humanoid deployment.

The QuadOcc ground truth is semi-automatic and depends on Grounded-SAM labels projected to LiDAR, temporal aggregation, and targeted manual fixes, but the paper does not provide a quantitative annotation-quality audit, inter-annotator check, or held-out manual validation. This is a material concern because the benchmark itself is a main contribution.

Several headline claims are somewhat overstated. On QuadOcc, the full dual-projection variant reaches only 20.56 mIoU and rare-class IoUs remain very low, e.g. pedestrian 2.86. The gain over MonoScene is modest (+1.37 mIoU), and the night result trails MonoScene in mIoU.

The 'lightweight' claim is mixed. On H3O the model is smaller than MonoScene, but on QuadOcc the dual-projection model has 189.8M parameters versus 148.9M for MonoScene, while dual projection adds only +0.53 mIoU over ER-only and increases parameters by 86.5% over ER-only.

Some baseline adaptations are substantial and may affect fairness. For example, VoxFormer query settings are reduced for efficiency, LMSCNet is widened 8x for the small grid, relation losses are disabled, and LiDAR baselines operate under a limited semantic setup. The paper documents these choices, but it remains hard to know whether each baseline is near its best attainable performance.

The comparison to LiDAR baselines should be interpreted cautiously. Camera methods receive rich RGB semantics, while LiDAR-only methods may be disadvantaged for semantic classification in this 6-class occupancy setting; therefore 'surpassing LiDAR' is not as strong as it sounds.

GDC is conceptually appealing but empirically weakly isolated: on QuadOcc it adds only +0.39 mIoU, is a global feature-level 2D displacement rather than a physically grounded gait model, and the paper provides limited direct evidence that it specifically compensates gait-induced jitter rather than acting as generic learned sampling refinement.

H3O is synthetic and its gait is modeled mainly through speed-conditioned vertical bobbing. This is useful for controlled evaluation but does not fully validate humanoid real-world panoramic occupancy, especially under complex roll/pitch, dynamic crowds, indoor settings, or camera/robot-specific artifacts.

strengths: The paper targets a meaningful and underexplored setting: semantic occupancy from a single 360-degree panoramic camera on legged or humanoid platforms, where body jitter, full-surround perception, and onboard constraints are genuinely relevant.

The dataset effort is potentially valuable. QuadOcc provides real quadruped panoramic data, and H3O provides a larger controlled synthetic benchmark with within-city and cross-city splits. If released with usable code and annotations, these could be useful to the community.

The manuscript contains substantial supplementary material, including baseline adaptation details, extra ablations, calibration-noise tests, temporal-fusion comparisons, runtime breakdowns, and dataset construction descriptions.

The proposed design is coherent at a high level: dual raw/equirectangular processing for PAL imagery, Cartesian plus cylindrical lifting for panoramic geometry, and a lightweight 3D decoder are reasonable choices for this problem.

On the reported benchmarks, OneOcc consistently improves over adapted vision baselines. The gains are especially large on H3O-Heter, where mIoU improves from 24.15 for MonoScene to 32.23, suggesting the design may improve cross-city generalization in the synthetic setting.
weaknesses: The core empirical case on the real benchmark is weak. On QuadOcc, OneOcc improves over MonoScene by only 1.37 mIoU, and the ablation gains are small: GDC adds 0.39, DP-ER adds 0.31, BGV adds 0.41, and AMoE-3D adds 0.26 mIoU. These margins are not accompanied by variance, multiple splits, or statistical analysis, so it is hard to judge whether the real-data improvement is robust.

Several claimed contributions appear incremental or weakly justified by evidence. GDC is described as gait displacement compensation, but it regresses a global 2D feature shift from a single image without direct motion supervision, and its gain is small and confounded with the change from integer gathering to bilinear sampling. AMoE-3D and BGV are plausible engineering additions, but the real-data evidence does not show a substantial effect.

The strongest gains are on H3O, which is synthetic. The paper positions the work around legged and humanoid robots, but the humanoid-style benchmark is CARLA-based and the authors acknowledge a sim-to-real gap. There is no real humanoid evaluation and no downstream robotic navigation, collision avoidance, or locomotion experiment to support the embodied-deployment claims.

The real dataset is limited in diversity and semantic granularity: QuadOcc has only 10 scenes, 6 classes, and a coarse 64x64x8 grid with 0.4 m voxels. This may be suitable for a first benchmark, but it constrains the strength of claims about general legged-robot perception, rare classes, thin structures, and real-world deployment.

The comparison to LiDAR baselines is not fully convincing. The paper emphasizes that OneOcc surpasses the best LiDAR baseline on QuadOcc, but the LiDAR methods are adapted classical SSC models under a very low-resolution near-field grid, while the proposed method is tailored to panoramic imagery and the dataset. The result is interesting but does not establish that vision-only panoramic SSC generally rivals LiDAR sensing for robotics.

The efficiency narrative is inconsistent. The H3O single-projection variant has 101.76M parameters, but the QuadOcc dual-projection model has 189.83M parameters, larger than MonoScene. The DP-ER ablation improves QuadOcc mIoU by only 0.53 while increasing parameters substantially, weakening the claim that the full real-data model is lightweight.

Ground-truth construction for QuadOcc relies on Grounded-SAM label transfer, LiDAR aggregation, semantic-guided mapping, and targeted manual fixes. This is a reasonable pipeline, but the paper does not provide enough quantitative annotation-quality validation, inter-annotator checks, or noise analysis. Since the reported real-data gains are small, label noise could materially affect conclusions.

Baseline adaptation details are extensive, but fairness remains difficult to assess. Many baselines were originally designed for different camera models, voxel conventions, and sensor modalities; some entries use predicted depth or LiDAR variants. The paper does not clearly separate improvements due to architecture from improvements due to retuning, panorama-specific preprocessing, and dataset-specific engineering.

Reproducibility is incomplete at review time. The paper says datasets and code will be publicly available, but the review must evaluate the submitted manuscript as-is. Without released data/code, the new benchmarks, annotation pipeline, and adapted baselines cannot be independently checked.

The presentation is overclaimed and sometimes imprecise. Terms such as jitter-robust, deployable, full-surround perception, and lightweight are used more strongly than the experiments justify. The manuscript is also very long and contains some formatting/language issues, though these are secondary to the evidentiary concerns.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and underexplored setting: semantic occupancy from a single panoramic camera on legged/humanoid platforms, where 360-degree continuity and gait-induced jitter are genuinely relevant and not well covered by standard autonomous-driving SSC benchmarks.

The technical design is well motivated for the sensing geometry. Dual raw/equirectangular projection, Cartesian plus cylindrical voxelization, feature-level gait displacement compensation, and a lightweight 3D decoder each address plausible failure modes of panoramic SSC.

The empirical evidence is fairly strong. OneOcc improves over adapted vision baselines on QuadOcc and H3O, with especially large gains on the cross-city H3O split (32.23 vs. 24.15 mIoU over MonoScene) and consistent component-wise gains in ablations.

The dataset contribution is valuable. QuadOcc provides real quadruped panoramic occupancy data, while H3O supplies controlled synthetic panoramic data with within-city and cross-city splits, weather/lighting variation, depth, semantics, poses, and two resolutions.

The supplementary material is unusually thorough: it includes module ablations, field-of-view studies, grid comparisons, calibration-noise robustness, temporal aggregation baselines, resolution scaling, Jetson runtime, dataset construction pipelines, and baseline adaptation details.
The authors are transparent about several limitations, including coarse voxel resolution, sim-to-real gap, moderate QuadOcc diversity, single-frame inference, and adverse-weather/night failure cases.
weaknesses: The main real-world benchmark is still limited in scope: QuadOcc has only 10 scenes, 6 semantic classes, a campus-like domain, and a coarse 64x64x8 grid at 0.4 m. This weakens claims about broad deployability on diverse legged/humanoid robots.

The humanoid evaluation is entirely simulated in CARLA. H3O is useful, but the large cross-city gains may not translate to real humanoid platforms because rendering, gait bobbing, dynamics, and occupancy labels are simulator-defined.

Ground-truth quality for QuadOcc depends on Grounded-SAM label initialization, LiDAR aggregation, temporal voting, and targeted manual fixes. The construction pipeline is plausible, but the paper does not provide an independent quantitative audit of annotation accuracy or inter-annotator/quality statistics beyond confidence-based curation.

Some claimed modules have modest isolated effects on the real benchmark: the total improvement over the MonoScene-like baseline on QuadOcc is +1.37 mIoU, with individual ablations of +0.26 to +0.41 mIoU. The architectural novelty is therefore more an effective integration of reasonable geometric biases than a single decisive algorithmic advance.

The gait displacement compensation claim is only partially substantiated. The ablation shows a small gain and qualitative offsets, but there is no direct evaluation against measured body motion, IMU/pose-derived jitter, different gait speeds, or failure cases where learned displacement is wrong.

Efficiency claims need qualification. On H3O the model is lighter than MonoScene, but on QuadOcc the full dual-projection variant has substantially more parameters than MonoScene (about 189.8M vs. 148.9M), so the 'lightweight' framing is configuration-dependent.

Baseline adaptation is carefully described, but fairness remains somewhat hard to judge because several baselines required nontrivial modifications, loss changes, grid changes, and in some cases altered proposal/depth routes. The paper would be stronger with released code/configs and possibly validation that each adapted baseline matches its original behavior on a known dataset.

The paper is dense and at times overclaims deployment readiness. The low mIoU values on rare classes, weaker nighttime results, coarse resolution, and static single-frame formulation suggest the method is promising for research benchmarking rather than yet a complete safety-critical robotics perception solution.
